newsitem.title: UK: Britain hints at Northern Irish prisoner release.
newsitem.headline: Britain hints at Northern Irish prisoner release.

text.p: A British minister hinted in remarks published on Sunday that the government might free prisoners jailed as a result of Northern Irish guerrilla activities if a three-week-old IRA ceasefire holds.

The remarks by Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam coincided with the 26th anniversary this weekend of an internment without trial policy which the government introduced to try to stamp out killings and bombings in the Irish Republican Army's campaign for an end to British rule in the province.
The draconian measure was dropped in the late 1970s.

Mowlam told the British Sunday Telegraph newspaper that she was not yet ready to consider demands by pro-British loyalist and pro-Irish republican guerrillas to free hundreds of activists jailed in the 28-year-old Northern Ireland conflict.
But she said that, if the July 20 ceasefire by the Irish Republican Army (IRA) held, "other options become possible".

Mowlam's remarks provided the clearest signal since she took office after the Labour Party's landslide general election victory on May 1 that the government might consider parole or remission for the convicted men and women who have helped prosecute a war in which about 3,200 people have died.
Previous British governments have ruled out any amnesty for prisoners, arguing that they are common criminals convicted of security offences, not political prisoners.
Mowlam's remarks were published as thousands of Roman Catholic Irish nationalists prepared to march in the province on the internment without trial anniversary.

Even though the practice has long since been abandoned, it remains a rallying point for both loyalist and republican activists who now sense that a sea change in British government attitudes to jailed colleagues is taking place.
On August 9, 1971, Northern Ireland police backed by British troops burst into homes across the province to detain hundreds of guerrilla suspects and put them in the Maze prison, near Belfast.

Mowlam linked progress on the estimated 600 prisoners from both camps to the maintenance of the ceasefire the IRA called which will allow its political wing, Sinn Fein, to join peace talks in December if the truce is deemed genuine.

She said that she would not be making her mind up on the IRA truce until the end of this month but added that intelligence reports suggested that the first two weeks of the ceasefire were "the clearest two weeks in memory."

Under British government terms, ceasefires by the IRA outlaw all guerrilla attacks as well as surveillance of potential targets and "punishment beatings" meted out by self-styled loyalist and republican police within their own communities.

Since July 20, there has been no violence directly linked to either the IRA or its loyalist adversaries, who called a ceasefire in October 1994 in a successful bid to get their political representatives to the peace negotiations.
But breakaway loyalist and republican guerrillas continue to be active, security sources say, and remain dangerous.

Police in Londonderry said at the weekend that an IRA breakaway group called the Continuity Army Council claimed credit for a series of hoax bomb alerts during a march by 12,000 members of the Protestant Apprentice Boys organisation.
Masked men, one armed with a handgun, hijacked a van and abandoned it on a bridge over which the marchers were due to pass. Army experts blew it up and found no bomb.

The Loyalist Volunteer Force, a breakaway group which says the Anglo-Irish peace process is designed to end British sovereignty over Northern Ireland, said in a weekend statement that it would bomb targets in Ireland.

A spokesman for the group, which is suspected of a string of bomb attacks, said the LVF had obtained Semtex plastic explosive and would hit Ireland unless Dublin dropped its constitutional claim to Northern Ireland and its people.

"We'll bomb (the cities of) Dublin, Cork, Galway, we are going as far south as we can," an LVF spokesman told the Sunday Mirror, a British weekly tabloid newspaper. "The whole of the south of Ireland is a target," he added.
